# MCP server grants

Source: https://docs.theauth.dev/mcp-grants

The MCP authorization server issues tokens for the authorization code flow by default. Four more ways to get a token are available, and all four are off until you configure them:

- `client_credentials`: a confidential client gets a token for itself, with no user involved.
- Token exchange (RFC 8693): trade an access token this server issued for a narrower one, optionally for another resource.
- `jwt-bearer` (RFC 7523): redeem an Identity Assertion JWT Authorization Grant (ID-JAG) signed by an identity provider you trust.
- `private_key_jwt`: authenticate a client with a signed assertion instead of a shared secret.

Everything here goes in the `config` object you pass to `createMcpModule`. See [MCP OAuth 2.1](/mcp) for the base setup.

## What changes in the metadata

Each enabled grant is added to `grant_types_supported` in the authorization server metadata. `private_key_jwt` and its algorithm list (`token_endpoint_auth_signing_alg_values_supported`) are always advertised. A grant that is not enabled answers `unsupported_grant_type`.

## Register the client for the grant

A client can only use a grant it is registered for. Through dynamic registration, list the grant type in `grant_types`:

| Grant | `grant_types` value |
| --- | --- |
| Client credentials | `client_credentials` |
| Token exchange | `urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:token-exchange` |
| jwt-bearer | `urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:jwt-bearer` |

Registration refuses a grant type that is not enabled on the server, and refuses `client_credentials` for a client with `token_endpoint_auth_method: "none"`. For clients you pre-register in config, set `grantTypes` on the entry in `preRegisteredClients`. The default there is `authorization_code` and `refresh_token` only.

<Warning>
  Open dynamic registration lets any caller create a client that lists these grants. The grants still need a `resolvePrincipal` mapping (client credentials), a trusted issuer (jwt-bearer) or a valid subject token (exchange), so registration alone gets nobody a token. If you do not want self-registered clients to be eligible at all, restrict `/mcp/register` or use pre-registered clients.
</Warning>

All three grants require a `resource` (RFC 8707) unless [`lenientClients.optionalResource`](/mcp-client-compat) is on and exactly one resource is configured. None of them issues a refresh token, and `offline_access` is never granted.

## client_credentials

```ts
import { createMcpModule } from "@glinr/theauth/mcp";

const mcp = createMcpModule({
  config: {
    // ...issuer, baseUrl, signingSecret, resource
    clientCredentials: {
      enabled: true,
      resolvePrincipal: async (client) => {
        const service = await db.findServiceByClientId(client.clientId);
        if (!service) return null; // refuse
        return {
          subject: `svc:${service.id}`, // becomes the token sub
          agentId: service.agentId,     // emitted as agent_id when set
          agentType: "autonomous",
          trustTier: "standard",
          scopes: ["mcp:read"],         // upper bound for this principal
        };
      },
    },
  },
  // ...your storage callbacks
});
```

`resolvePrincipal` is required. Without it no client can obtain a token, so a client created through open registration is not enough on its own.

The token request:

```http
POST /api/auth/mcp/token
Authorization: Basic base64(client_id:client_secret)
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

grant_type=client_credentials&scope=mcp:read&resource=https://mcp.example.com
```

Rules:

- The client must be confidential: a secret (`client_secret_basic` or `client_secret_post`) or `private_key_jwt`.
- The token `sub` is the principal's `subject`, never a user.
- Scopes are bounded by `principal.scopes`, falling back to the client's registered `scope`. With neither, the request fails with `invalid_scope`. A request can narrow within that bound, never widen.
- No refresh token is issued. Send a DPoP proof and the token is bound to that key (`token_type: "DPoP"`).

## Token exchange (RFC 8693)

```ts
import { createInMemoryJtiDenylist } from "@glinr/theauth/mcp";

const mcp = createMcpModule({
  config: {
    // ...
    jtiDenylist: createInMemoryJtiDenylist(), // required with tokenExchange
    tokenExchange: {
      enabled: true,
      maxChainDepth: 3, // default
      authorize: async ({ client, subject, scopes, resource }) => {
        return client.clientId === "orchestrator" && scopes.every((s) => s.startsWith("mcp:"));
      },
    },
  },
  // ...
});
```

Clients that authenticate with `private_key_jwt` can also revoke tokens through `mcp.revoke(request)`. The framework adapters do not serve `/mcp/revoke` themselves, so mount a `POST` route in your host that calls `mcp.revoke(request)` (see [MCP](/mcp)); metadata advertises `<baseUrl>/mcp/revoke`, so mount it there. The assertion audience must be the revoke endpoint URL or the issuer, an assertion addressed to the token endpoint is refused there, and the `jti` store is shared with the token endpoint. An assertion combined with basic auth or `client_secret` is rejected.

`createMcpModule` throws at startup if `tokenExchange.enabled` is set without `jtiDenylist`. The denylist is what makes a revoked subject token fail the exchange. See the multi-instance note below.

The request carries a `subject_token` (and optionally an `actor_token`), both with `..._token_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:access_token`. Only access tokens issued by this server are accepted. Other token types are rejected with `invalid_request`.

```http
grant_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:token-exchange
&subject_token=eyJ...
&subject_token_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:access_token
&scope=mcp:read
&resource=https://tools.example.com
```

What the server enforces:

| Rule | Behavior |
| --- | --- |
| Subject and actor tokens | Must verify, be unexpired and not be on the denylist. |
| Scope | Narrow only. Anything outside the subject token's scopes is `invalid_scope`. |
| Audience | Unchanged, or another configured resource (`resource` or `audience`). Otherwise `invalid_target`. |
| Lifetime | The new token never outlives the subject token. |
| DPoP | A bound subject token needs a proof from the same key, and the new token carries that binding. |
| Delegation chain | The new token gets a nested `act` claim, capped at `maxChainDepth` hops (default 3). |
| Policy | `authorize` returning `false` refuses with `access_denied`. |

The `act` claim names the actor: the actor token's user and client when you send one, otherwise the exchanging client. Earlier hops are nested inside it, and resource servers see them as `principal.delegationChain` (see [DPoP and requireMcpAuth](/dpop)). The response includes `issued_token_type`.

## jwt-bearer and ID-JAG (RFC 7523)

An enterprise identity provider signs an assertion that says "this user may use this client at this resource". The client redeems it at the token endpoint.

```ts
const mcp = createMcpModule({
  config: {
    // ...
    jwtBearer: {
      enabled: true,
      trustedIssuers: [
        {
          issuer: "https://idp.corp.example",
          jwksUri: "https://idp.corp.example/.well-known/jwks.json",
        },
      ],
      mapSubject: async ({ issuer, subject, clientId, scopes }) => {
        const user = await db.findUserByEmail(subject);
        return user?.id ?? null; // null refuses the grant
      },
      // algs: ["ES256", "ES384", "EdDSA", "PS256", "RS256"], // default
      // maxLifetimeSeconds: 300,                              // default
      // clockSkewSeconds: 30,                                 // default
    },
  },
  // ...
});
```

`trustedIssuers` must have at least one entry and `mapSubject` is required, or startup throws. Each issuer takes `jwksUri` (HTTPS, fetched through the SSRF-safe fetcher), static `jwks`, or both. Static keys are tried first, and a `jwksUri` is consulted when no static key matches. Fetched key sets are cached in process for five minutes, and an unknown `kid` triggers at most one refetch every 30 seconds. If a refetch fails, the stale copy is used for up to 30 minutes.

The assertion must have JOSE header `typ: oauth-id-jag+jwt` and claims `iss`, `sub`, `aud`, `exp`, `iat`, `jti` and `client_id`. The checks:

- `iss` is one of the trusted issuers, and the signature verifies against its keys.
- `aud` equals this server's `issuer`.
- `client_id` equals the authenticated client.
- `exp - iat` is at most `maxLifetimeSeconds`.
- `jti` has not been seen from that issuer. Replays are tracked in `assertionStorage`.
- An optional `scope` claim bounds the scopes (default `openid`), and an optional `resource` claim must agree with the request.

```http
grant_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:jwt-bearer
&assertion=eyJ...
&resource=https://mcp.example.com
```

## private_key_jwt client authentication

Register the client with public keys instead of a secret:

```json
{
  "redirect_uris": [],
  "grant_types": ["client_credentials"],
  "token_endpoint_auth_method": "private_key_jwt",
  "jwks_uri": "https://agent.example.com/.well-known/jwks.json"
}
```

Give exactly one of `jwks` (public keys only, private members are refused) or `jwks_uri` (public HTTPS). Client ID Metadata Documents can declare `private_key_jwt` too. No secret is generated for these clients.

At the token endpoint the client sends `client_assertion_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:client-assertion-type:jwt-bearer` and a `client_assertion`. The assertion must have:

- `iss` and `sub` both equal to the `client_id`.
- `aud` equal to the token endpoint URL (`dpop.tokenEndpointUrl`, else `<baseUrl>/mcp/token`) or the issuer.
- `exp` no more than 300 seconds out (30 seconds of skew allowed), and a `jti`.
- A signature in ES256, ES384, EdDSA, PS256 or RS256. HMAC and `none` are never accepted.

Each `jti` works once per client. Do not send a `client_secret` or Basic header alongside an assertion: the request is refused.

## Multi-instance deployments

Two stores default to process memory and break down behind a load balancer.

**`jtiDenylist`.** `createInMemoryJtiDenylist()` is per process. A token revoked through `mcp.revoke` on one instance still exchanges on another. Pass your own `McpJtiDenylist` (`revoke(jti, expiresAt)` and `isRevoked(jti)`) backed by Redis or your database.

**`assertionStorage`.** The replay cache for `private_key_jwt` assertions and jwt-bearer `jti` values defaults to an in-process store. With several instances an assertion can be replayed once per instance. Give every instance the same shared store:

```ts
const theauth = await createTheAuth({
  // ...
  secondaryStorage: "database", // or a Redis storage
});

const mcp = createMcpModule({
  config: {
    // ...
    assertionStorage: theauth.secondaryStorage.for("nonces"),
  },
  // ...
});
```

Replay protection is only as strict as the store's `incr`. Cloudflare KV is not atomic (`atomicIncr` is `false`), so two simultaneous replays can both pass there.

# MCP client compatibility

Source: https://docs.theauth.dev/mcp-client-compat

Some MCP clients do not follow the strict shape the authorization server enforces by default. They leave out `resource`, ask for vendor scopes the server has never heard of, redirect to a loopback address on a random port, or name a sub-path of your MCP server as the audience. By default every one of those is an error.

`lenientClients` turns individual relaxations on, one at a time. Every option is off unless you set it, which is the strict behavior described in [MCP OAuth 2.1](/mcp).

```ts
import { createMcpModule } from "@glinr/theauth/mcp";

const mcp = createMcpModule({
  config: {
    // ...issuer, baseUrl, signingSecret, resource
    lenientClients: {
      optionalResource: true,
      pathAudience: true,
      dropUnknownScopes: true,
      loopbackAnyPort: true,
    },
  },
  // ...your storage callbacks
});
```

## Options

| Option | Relaxes | Default |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `optionalResource` | A missing `resource` parameter | off |
| `dropUnknownScopes` | Rejecting scopes the server does not support | off |
| `loopbackAnyPort` | Exact match of loopback redirect URIs | off |
| `loopbackAllowLocalhost` | Adds `http://localhost` to `loopbackAnyPort` | off |
| `pathAudience` | Exact match of the `resource` value | off |

### optionalResource

When `resource` is missing at the authorize endpoint or in an authorization code exchange, it defaults to the one configured resource (`allowedResources` when set, otherwise `resource`). With zero or several configured resources, a missing value is still `invalid_target`. A `resource` that is present but not allowed is always `invalid_target`. It also lets the non-interactive grants (client credentials, jwt-bearer) fall back to the same single resource.

Tradeoff: low. The audience can only ever be a resource you configured, and with a single one there is nothing to be ambiguous about.

### dropUnknownScopes

A requested scope the server does not support is dropped instead of failing the request. The supported set is the defaults (`openid`, `profile`, `email`, `offline_access`) plus `config.scopes`. The granted scope comes back in the token response, and the request only fails with `invalid_scope` when scopes were requested and none are left. On a refresh, scopes outside the original grant are dropped the same way, so a refresh cannot widen.

Tradeoff: medium. A client no longer finds out from an error that it asked for something wrong, and it may receive less than it expected. It can never receive more than the server supports and its registration allows. Clients must read the returned `scope` instead of assuming.

### loopbackAnyPort

RFC 8252 section 7.3. When a registered redirect URI is `http://127.0.0.1` or `http://[::1]`, a request matches if scheme, host, path and query are identical and only the port differs. `127.0.0.1` and `[::1]` do not match each other, and URIs with a fragment or userinfo never match. `localhost` is excluded unless `loopbackAllowLocalhost` is also set.

Tradeoff: higher. Any process on the user's machine can listen on a port and receive the redirect. PKCE S256 is what stops that process from redeeming the code, and this server requires PKCE for every client. Do not enable this for a client that cannot do S256. It only affects clients that registered a loopback URI.

### pathAudience

A requested `resource` matches a configured one when the two are equal apart from a trailing slash, or when the configured value is a path prefix of the request on a `/` boundary. `https://api.example.com/mcp/sse` matches `https://api.example.com/mcp`, and `https://api.example.com/mcp-admin` does not. Requests carrying a query or fragment never match. When several configured resources match, the longest wins. The issued token's `aud` is always the configured resource, never the sub-path.

Tradeoff: low to medium. A client can get a token for the whole configured resource while naming one sub-path, so do not rely on the sub-path to narrow what the token allows.

## Recommended profile

For a single-resource MCP server that public clients (Client ID Metadata Documents or dynamic registration) connect to:

```ts
lenientClients: {
  optionalResource: true,   // many clients omit resource
  pathAudience: true,       // clients address /mcp/sse or /mcp/messages
  dropUnknownScopes: true,  // vendor scopes the server does not list
  loopbackAnyPort: true,    // native clients use ephemeral ports
},
clientIdMetadataDocuments: {
  enabled: true,
  allowedHosts: ["clients.example.com"], // hosts whose client metadata you accept
},
```

Leave `loopbackAllowLocalhost` off unless a client you must support registers `http://localhost/...`. If you only serve clients that behave, enable none of these. The strict defaults are the safer ones, and each switch is easy to add later when a specific client needs it.

## Differences from the Go library

The Go library has the same five switches as `ClientCompat` (`OptionalResource`, `DropUnknownScopes`, `LoopbackAnyPort`, `LoopbackAllowLocalhost`, `PathAudience`). See [Client compatibility profile](/go/guides/client-compat) for its documentation. The meaning matches, with these differences:

- **Scope source.** Go keeps a scope only if it is in the resource catalog and in the client's registered scope. The TypeScript server checks the server's supported set (defaults plus `config.scopes`) at the authorize endpoint. Grants that are bounded by a registered scope or principal still enforce that bound.
- **Path audience strictness.** Go also refuses userinfo, dot segments and percent-encoded dots or slashes in the requested resource. The TypeScript check compares origin and path after URL parsing and refuses a query or fragment.
- **jwt-bearer.** Go compares the raw `resource` of an ID-JAG assertion and does not accept sub-paths there. TypeScript canonicalizes both the claim and the request value.
- **No PAR.** The TypeScript server has no pushed authorization requests, so `optionalResource` applies at authorize and token only.

# OAuth 2.1 and MCP conformance test

Source: https://docs.theauth.dev/conformance

Black-box checks for any OAuth 2.1 authorization server or MCP resource server. Each check passes, fails or skips. No secrets needed.

```bash
npx @glinr/theauth-conformance https://auth.example.com
```

## Conformance command options

```text
theauth-conformance <url> [options]

  --json                 Print the report as JSON
  --badge <file>         Write a shields.io endpoint badge JSON file
  --resource <url>       Protected MCP endpoint to probe for the 401 challenge
  --client-id <id>       Use this client instead of registering one through DCR
  --redirect-uri <uri>   Redirect URI registered for --client-id
  --token <token>        Access token, only read to inspect its audience
  --refresh-token <tok>  Refresh token for the rotation check (it gets consumed)
  --timeout <ms>         Per-request timeout, default 10000
  --verbose              Include evidence in the human report
  --strict               Exit 1 on any failed check, not only MUST failures
```

The tool checks the `/.well-known` metadata paths for authorization servers and protected resources. Set `THEAUTH_CONFORMANCE_TOKEN` and `THEAUTH_CONFORMANCE_REFRESH_TOKEN` to keep tokens out of shell history.

| Exit code | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `0` | No MUST check failed |
| `1` | A MUST check failed (any failed check with `--strict`) |
| `2` | Usage error |

## Checks

Severity follows RFC 2119. A failed MUST turns the badge red. A failed SHOULD or MAY turns it yellow.

| Check id | Severity | Spec | Verifies |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `as-metadata` | must | RFC 8414 | Issuer matches, endpoints https |
| `rs-metadata` | should | RFC 9728 | Names an authorization server |
| `metadata-consistency` | must | RFC 9728, RFC 8414 | Issuer and scopes agree |
| `pkce-s256-advertised` | must | OAuth 2.1, RFC 7636 | `S256` advertised, `plain` not |
| `pkce-required` | must | OAuth 2.1, RFC 9700 | No `code_challenge` is refused |
| `pkce-plain-rejected` | must | OAuth 2.1, RFC 7636 | `plain` method is refused |
| `redirect-exact-match` | must | OAuth 2.1, RFC 9700 | Altered or foreign URI never followed |
| `dcr-registration` | should | RFC 7591 | Public client registers (201) |
| `dcr-validation` | must | RFC 7591 | Plain http and `javascript:` refused |
| `refresh-garbage-rejected` | must | RFC 6749, OAuth 2.1 | Made-up refresh token refused |
| `refresh-rotation` | must | OAuth 2.1, RFC 9700 | Rotates, old token refused, replay revokes |
| `resource-indicator-audience` | must | RFC 8707 | JWT `aud` matches resource |
| `token-exchange-rejects-garbage` | must | RFC 8693 | Made-up subject token refused |
| `token-exchange-act-chain` | should | RFC 8693 | Nested `act` claims. Always skipped. |
| `introspection-inactive` | must | RFC 7662 | Garbage token gives `active=false` |
| `dpop-advertised` | may | RFC 9449 | Asymmetric algorithms only |
| `dpop-enforced` | must | RFC 9449 | Garbage proof gets 401 |
| `www-authenticate-resource-metadata` | must | RFC 9728, RFC 6750 | 401 has working `resource_metadata` |

Skips are never faked into passes, and each one says why.

## Skipped checks

- Not advertised: DCR, token exchange, introspection, DPoP.
- `refresh-rotation`: needs `--refresh-token` and `--client-id`. The test consumes the token.
- `resource-indicator-audience`: needs `--token` (a JWT).
- `token-exchange-act-chain`: needs a valid subject token and client credentials.
- Introspection behind client authentication (401 or 403).
- Negative authorize probes: the server never accepts a valid request, or shows a login page for the bad one. Skipped if the control request is rejected.

## Badge

`--badge out.json` writes a [shields.io endpoint](https://shields.io/badges/endpoint-badge):

```json
{
  "schemaVersion": 1,
  "label": "agent-auth",
  "message": "13/13 passed, 5 skipped",
  "color": "brightgreen"
}
```

Host the JSON at a stable public URL and point shields at it:

```markdown
[![agent-auth conformance](https://img.shields.io/endpoint?url=https%3A%2F%2Fexample.com%2Fagent-auth-badge.json)](https://docs.theauth.dev/conformance)
```

Refresh it in CI with `npx @glinr/theauth-conformance https://auth.example.com --badge badge.json`.

Only checks that ran count toward the message. Green: nothing failed. Yellow: only SHOULD or MAY failed. Red: a MUST failed. Grey (`not tested`): nothing could run.

## Use in code

```ts
import { buildBadge, runSuite } from "@glinr/theauth-conformance";

const report = await runSuite({ target: "https://auth.example.com", timeoutMs: 10000 });
const badge = buildBadge(report);
```

## Tested against theAuth

The package test runs the suite against the real MCP OAuth module from `@glinr/theauth` on a Node `http` server. Pinned result: 13 pass, 0 fail, 5 skipped (refresh rotation, audience, token exchange twice, introspection). A lax stub server must fail the checks.

## Limits

- A green badge means the server behaved correctly on these probes. It is not an audit.
- Skips never count as passes.

# Admin MCP server for theAuth deployments

Source: https://docs.theauth.dev/admin-mcp

The `@glinr/theauth-mcp` server is read-only by default. Add `--allow-writes` (or set `THEAUTH_ALLOW_WRITES=1`) to register four write tools. Each write needs human approval.

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "theauth-admin": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "@glinr/theauth-mcp", "--allow-writes"],
      "env": {
        "THEAUTH_API_URL": "https://auth.example.com/api",
        "THEAUTH_API_KEY": "...",
        "THEAUTH_MCP_ACTOR": "ops-bot@example.com"
      }
    }
  }
}
```

## Read tools

Always registered: `list_agents`, `get_agent`, `list_delegations`, `list_sessions`, `query_audit`, `check_permission`, `inspect_token`, `doctor` and `get_approval_status`. Tokens and secret-looking fields are redacted.

## Write tools

| Tool | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `revoke_agent` | Revoke an agent identity |
| `revoke_delegation` | Revoke a delegation chain |
| `rotate_key` | Rotate an agent credential. The new token is not shown to the client. |
| `disable_user` | Disable a user and end its sessions |

## Approval flow

Writes use the [approval flow](/approval). No write runs on the first call.

<Steps>

<Step>

### Request

The client calls the tool with the target `id`. The server logs the request, opens an approval (for example `admin:revoke_agent` on `agent:abc`) and returns `{ "status": "pending", "approvalId": "..." }`.

</Step>

<Step>

### Approve

A human approves or denies through your normal approval channel.

</Step>

<Step>

### Retry

The client polls `get_approval_status`, or calls the same tool again with `approvalId`.

</Step>

<Step>

### Run

If the approval is approved and unexpired, the server spends it and runs the change. Otherwise nothing runs.

</Step>

</Steps>

## Audit

With `THEAUTH_MCP_ACTOR` set (default `theauth-mcp`), every call is logged as `admin_mcp.<tool>` with that actor. Writes log each step: requested, pending, executed, denied or failed.

## Deployment routes

Core ships these routes as an opt-in plugin, `adminApi`. It is off unless `enabled` is exactly `true`. When it is off, every route answers 404.

```ts
import { adminApi, createTheAuth } from "@glinr/theauth";

const theauth = await createTheAuth({
  // ...
  plugins: [
    adminApi({
      enabled: true,
      adminUserIds: ["user_ops"],
      systemAgentId: "agent_admin_mcp",
      rateLimit: { max: 60, window: 60 },
    }),
  ],
});
```

| Route | Backed by |
| --- | --- |
| `GET /delegations` | Delegation chains, filtered by `agentId` and `status` |
| `DELETE /delegations/{id}` | `revokeDelegation` (cascades to child chains) |
| `GET /sessions` | Sessions as one-way `ref`s, never ids or tokens |
| `POST /users/{id}/disable` | Admin `banUser` (ends sessions, revokes agent tokens) |
| `POST /approvals` | `approval.request` |
| `GET /approvals/{id}` | `approval.get` |
| `POST /approvals/{id}/consume` | `consumeApproval`. A replay or race is refused with 409. |
| `POST /audit/events` | `recordAuditEvent`, secret-looking params redacted |

## Limits

- Calls need an `Authorization: Bearer` credential for a user in `adminUserIds`. Bad credentials get 401, other users get 403, and an empty list refuses everyone. Cookie-only requests are refused.
- `systemAgentId` must be an existing agent. The `agentId` and `userId` the MCP server sends are labels and are ignored. The approval belongs to the calling admin.
- Approval actions must look like `admin:<name>`. Only the admin who opened an approval can consume it. Approving still happens outside these routes.
- An approval is single use and tied to one action and one resource.
- If the audit write for a new request fails, the request is not opened.
- Admins cannot disable themselves or other configured admins, unless `allowDisablingAdmins` is set.
- Requests are rate limited per admin user. Ids, enums and body sizes are validated.

# DPoP and requireMcpAuth

Source: https://docs.theauth.dev/dpop

A bearer token works for whoever holds it. If an agent's token leaks from a log or a proxy, the thief can call your tools. DPoP closes that gap: the token carries the thumbprint of a key the client holds, and every request has to include a short-lived proof signed with that key.

DPoP is opt-in. Without `dpop` in your MCP config nothing changes.

## Turn it on

```ts
import { createMcpModule } from "@glinr/theauth/mcp";

const mcp = createMcpModule({
  config: {
    enabled: true,
    issuer: "https://auth.example.com",
    baseUrl: "https://auth.example.com/api/auth",
    signingSecret: process.env.MCP_SIGNING_SECRET!,
    resource: "https://mcp.example.com",
    dpop: {
      // required: true,        // refuse unbound tokens everywhere
      // requireNonce: true,    // server nonces (RFC 9449 section 8 and 9)
      storage: theauth.secondaryStorage.for("nonces"), // shared replay cache
    },
  },
  // ...your storage callbacks
});
```

| Option | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `algs` | ES256, ES384, EdDSA, PS256 | Accepted proof algorithms. |
| `required` | false | Every token request needs a proof, and resources refuse unbound tokens. |
| `proofMaxAgeSeconds` | 300 | Oldest accepted `iat`. |
| `clockSkewSeconds` | 30 | Allowed skew in both directions. |
| `requireNonce` | false | Proofs must carry a server nonce. |
| `nonceTtlSeconds` | 300 | Nonce lifetime. |
| `storage` | in-process memory | Replay cache and nonces. Use a shared store with more than one instance. |
| `tokenEndpointUrl` | `<baseUrl>/mcp/token` | The `htu` clients sign for the token endpoint. |

Both metadata documents then list `dpop_signing_alg_values_supported`. The protected resource document also sets `dpop_bound_access_tokens_required` when `required` is on.

## What the token endpoint does

When a request carries a `DPoP` header, the endpoint verifies the proof (`typ`, algorithm, public `jwk`, signature, `htm`, `htu`, `iat`, `jti` replay) and issues an access token with `cnf: { jkt }` and `token_type: "DPoP"`. Without a header you get a normal bearer token, unless `required` is set. The non-interactive grants (client credentials, token exchange, jwt-bearer) honor the proof the same way. See [MCP server grants](/mcp-grants).

The proof is checked before the authorization code is consumed. When `requireNonce` is on and the proof has no valid nonce, the endpoint answers `400 use_dpop_nonce` with a `DPoP-Nonce` header and leaves the code alone, so the client retries with the same code and a fresh proof.

Refresh tokens inherit the binding. A refresh request signed by a different key is refused before the token rotates, so a thief cannot burn the real client's token. Your `storeToken` callback should persist `dpopJkt` from the stored record, otherwise the binding is lost on refresh.

The built-in `createMcpResponseHelpers(...).tokenResponse` and every framework adapter copy the nonce into the `DPoP-Nonce` header. If you write your own token route, read `result.error.details?.dpopNonce`.

## Protect a handler

`requireMcpAuth` wraps any `(Request) => Response` function. It accepts `Authorization: Bearer` and, with DPoP enabled, `Authorization: DPoP`.

```ts
// Resource server
const tools = mcp.requireMcpAuth(
  async (request, principal) => {
    return Response.json({
      user: principal.userId,
      agent: principal.agent?.id ?? null,
      chain: principal.delegationChain,
      scheme: principal.scheme,
    });
  },
  { requiredScopes: ["mcp:read"] },
);

// Works anywhere that speaks Web Request/Response, for example Hono:
// app.all("/tools", (c) => tools(c.req.raw));
```

The client sends `Authorization: DPoP <token>` plus `DPoP: <proof>` where the proof is signed for the exact method and URL and includes `ath`, the base64url SHA-256 of the token. Use a new `jti` every time. The [client helper](#client-helper) below does all of that for you.

### What gets checked

- Token: signature, issuer, expiry, audience against `expectedAudience` or `McpConfig.resource`, the jti denylist.
- Proof: `htm`, `htu` (query and fragment ignored), `iat` window, `ath`, nonce, `jti` not seen before, and the proof key matching `cnf.jkt`.
- Bearer downgrade: a bound token sent as `Bearer` is refused. This also covers `validateToken`, `middleware`, `withMcpAuth` and `requireScopes`.
- A `DPoP` scheme request carrying an unbound token is refused.
- Scopes: a shortfall returns 403 `insufficient_scope`.

Options: `requiredScopes`, `expectedAudience`, `resourceUrl` (the public URL clients sign, for proxies), `resourceMetadataUrl`, `requireDpop`, `requireNonce`.

### Challenges

With no credentials the response is 401 with `Bearer resource_metadata="..."` and, if DPoP is on, a second `DPoP algs="ES256 ...", resource_metadata="..."` header. Bad tokens return `error="invalid_token"`, bad proofs `error="invalid_dpop_proof"`, and a missing nonce `error="use_dpop_nonce"` with a `DPoP-Nonce` header. The `resource_metadata` URL points at the RFC 9728 document so MCP clients can find your authorization server.

### The principal

| Field | Source |
| --- | --- |
| `userId`, `clientId`, `scopes`, `resource`, `tokenId`, `expiresAt` | Token claims |
| `agent` | `agent_id`, `agent_type`, `trust_tier` (needs `emitAgenticJwtClaims`) |
| `delegationChain` | Nested RFC 8693 `act` claims, current actor first |
| `scheme`, `dpopJkt` | How the caller authenticated |

## Client helper

`@glinr/theauth-client` ships `createDPoPClient` and `createDPoPProver`. They use WebCrypto only, so they run in browsers, Node, Bun, Deno and edge runtimes. Both sign with ES256.

```ts
import { createDPoPClient } from "@glinr/theauth-client";

const dpop = await createDPoPClient(); // generates a P-256 key pair

// 1. Token endpoint. The helper adds the DPoP header and handles the nonce challenge.
const tokenRes = await dpop.fetch("https://auth.example.com/api/auth/mcp/token", {
  method: "POST",
  headers: { "Content-Type": "application/x-www-form-urlencoded" },
  body: new URLSearchParams({
    grant_type: "authorization_code",
    code,
    code_verifier: verifier,
    client_id: clientId,
    redirect_uri: redirectUri,
    resource: "https://mcp.example.com",
  }),
});
const { access_token } = await tokenRes.json();

// 2. Resource request. Sends `Authorization: DPoP <token>` and a proof with `ath`.
const res = await dpop.fetch(
  "https://mcp.example.com/tools",
  { method: "POST", body: JSON.stringify({ tool: "list_repos" }) },
  { accessToken: access_token },
);
```

What it does on each call:

- Builds a proof with `htm`, a normalized `htu` (scheme, host and path, query and fragment dropped), `iat`, a fresh `jti`, `ath` when there is an access token, and `nonce` when one is cached for the origin.
- Sets `Authorization: DPoP <token>` when an access token is given, per request through the third argument or as the `accessToken` option (a string or a function).
- Reads `DPoP-Nonce` from every response and caches it per origin.
- On a `use_dpop_nonce` challenge (a 400 or 401 with a `DPoP-Nonce` header) it retries once with the new nonce and a new proof.

### Nonce flow

With `dpop.requireNonce` on the server, the first request has no nonce:

1. The client sends a proof without a nonce.
2. The server answers `400 use_dpop_nonce` (token endpoint) or `401` with `WWW-Authenticate: DPoP error="use_dpop_nonce"` (resource), plus a `DPoP-Nonce` header. The authorization code is not consumed.
3. The helper stores the nonce, signs a new proof that carries it, and retries once.
4. Later requests to the same origin send the cached nonce. When the server rotates it, the same challenge repeats.

The retry happens once per call. If the second attempt is also a challenge, the response is returned to you.

### Keys

The generated private key is non-extractable and lives only as long as the object. A token is bound to that key, so keep using the same one for refresh. To persist it, pass your own key pair, for example one you store in IndexedDB:

```ts
const dpop = await createDPoPClient({ keyPair: storedKeyPair }); // ECDSA P-256 CryptoKeyPair
const jkt = await dpop.thumbprint(); // the cnf.jkt value the server binds to
```

Use `createDPoPProver` when you only need proofs and want to send the request yourself. It exposes `createProof({ method, url, accessToken?, nonce? })`, `thumbprint()`, `publicJwk`, `getNonce(url)` and `setNonce(url, nonce)`. Share one prover between a token client and a resource client with `createDPoPClient({ prover })` so both use the same key and nonce cache.

## Adapters and CORS

The token endpoint returns the nonce in `error.details.dpopNonce`. All ten framework adapters (Express, Fastify, Hono, NestJS, Next.js, Nuxt, SvelteKit, SolidStart, TanStack and Astro) copy it into the `DPoP-Nonce` response header on `/mcp/token` errors, so the retry works through any of them. Before this, only the Hono and Express adapters did.

The adapters' MCP CORS headers also allow the `DPoP` request header and expose `DPoP-Nonce` and `WWW-Authenticate`, which a browser client needs to read the challenge. If you serve the token endpoint some other way, set the same headers yourself.

## Limits

- The replay cache is only as strict as its store. Cloudflare KV is not atomic, so two simultaneous replays can both pass. Use Redis or the database store when that matters.
- The `dpop_jkt` authorization request parameter (binding the code to a key up front) is not implemented. The binding starts at the token request.
- Unbound refresh tokens issued before you enabled DPoP are bound to whatever key first refreshes them. Rotate them out by setting `required` after a refresh cycle.

# Reverse proxy gateway for AI agent auth

Source: https://docs.theauth.dev/gateway

```bash
npx @glinr/theauth-gateway --config gateway.json --database ./theauth.db --port 3000
```

Needs Node 20 or newer. For MCP servers, use [Gateway for MCP servers](/gateway-mcp).

<Steps>
<Step>

### Create an agent

Create it in the gateway's SQLite file. Keep `agent.token`.

```typescript
import { createTheAuth } from '@glinr/theauth';

const theauth = await createTheAuth({
  database: { provider: 'sqlite', url: './theauth.db' },
  agents: { enabled: true },
});

const agent = await theauth.agent.create({
  ownerId: 'user-1', // must be an existing user id
  name: 'support-bot',
  type: 'autonomous',
  permissions: [{ resource: 'api', actions: ['read'] }],
});
console.log(agent.token);
```

</Step>
<Step>

### Write gateway.json

```json
{
  "upstream": "http://localhost:8080",
  "policies": [
    { "path": "/health", "public": true },
    {
      "path": "/api/**",
      "method": "GET",
      "requiredPermissions": [{ "resource": "api", "actions": ["read"] }]
    },
    {
      "path": "/api/**",
      "requiredPermissions": [{ "resource": "api", "actions": ["write"] }]
    }
  ],
  "rateLimit": { "windowMs": 60000, "max": 100 }
}
```

</Step>
<Step>

### Start and call

Run the command at the top, then:

```bash
curl http://localhost:3000/api/items                                         # 401
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $AGENT_TOKEN" http://localhost:3000/api/items # proxied
```

</Step>
</Steps>

<Warning>
The default `--database` is `:memory:`, so protected requests get 401. The CLI is SQLite only.
</Warning>

## Request order

The first matching policy wins.

| Step | Check | On failure |
|------|-------|------------|
| 1 | `/_theauth/health`, then CORS preflight | None |
| 2 | First policy matching path glob and method | Still needs a token, but no permission check or route limit |
| 3 | Agent token, unless `public` or `requireAuth: false` | 401, `WWW-Authenticate: Bearer` |
| 4 | Global and policy rate limits | 429, `Retry-After` |
| 5 | Every `requiredPermissions` pair | 403 |
| 6 | Forward, then audit | None |

Error codes: `UNAUTHORIZED`, `FORBIDDEN`, `RATE_LIMITED`, `PAYLOAD_TOO_LARGE`, `BAD_GATEWAY`, `GATEWAY_TIMEOUT`.

## Always on

| Behavior | Detail |
|----------|--------|
| Fixed upstream | Clients cannot pick a host. Only `http` and `https`, no embedded credentials. |
| Tokens stripped (breaking) | `Authorization` and `DPoP` are removed. Keep them with `--forward-auth` or `stripAuthHeader: false`. |
| Headers | Client `Forwarded`, `X-Forwarded-*` and `X-Real-IP` are dropped. `X-Forwarded-For` comes only from `trustedProxy`. |
| Redirects | Not followed. Upstream `Location` is rewritten to the gateway. |
| Body and timeout | Over `maxBodyBytes` gets 413. No headers within `upstreamTimeoutMs` gets 504. |
| Streaming | SSE and streamable HTTP pass through. A disconnect cancels the upstream. |
| 502 | Says only that the upstream is unreachable. |

## CLI flags

| Flag | Default | Purpose |
|------|---------|---------|
| `--upstream`, `-u` | required | Upstream URL |
| `--port`, `-p` | `3000` | Listen port |
| `--database`, `-d` | `:memory:` | SQLite path |
| `--config`, `-c` | none | `gateway.json` path |
| `--forward-auth` | off | Send `Authorization` upstream |
| `--no-audit` | off | Audit off |
| `--max-body-bytes` | `10485760` | Body cap, 10 MiB |
| `--trusted-proxy-count` | `0` | Proxies in front |
| `--trusted-header` | none | Edge header, such as `cf-connecting-ip` |
| `--mcp-resource`, `--mcp-issuer`, `--mcp-scope` | none | [MCP mode](/gateway-mcp) |

`--strip-auth` is still accepted and does nothing.

## gateway.json

```jsonc
{
  "upstream": "http://localhost:8080",         // required, http or https only
  "audit": true,
  "stripAuthHeader": true,                     // false keeps Authorization upstream
  "maxBodyBytes": 5242880,                     // default 10485760 (10 MiB)
  "upstreamTimeoutMs": 15000,                  // default 30000 (30 s for headers)
  "cors": { "origins": ["https://app.example.com"], "credentials": true }, // unlisted callers never get the first origin
  "rateLimit": { "windowMs": 60000, "max": 100 }, // per agent, or per client on anonymous routes
  "trustedProxy": { "trustedProxyCount": 1 },
  // "mcp" turns on MCP mode. "basePath" is accepted but has no effect on routing.
  "policies": [
    { "path": "/health", "public": true },     // micromatch: /api/* one level, /api/** any depth
    {
      "path": "/api/**",
      // requiredPermissions checks the agent's own permissions only, not delegated ones
      "requiredPermissions": [{ "resource": "api", "actions": ["read", "write"] }],
      "rateLimit": { "windowMs": 60000, "max": 20 }
    }
  ]
}
```

Policy fields: `path`, `method`, `public`, `requireAuth`, `requiredPermissions`, `requiredScopes` (MCP only), `rateLimit`. Validated on start.

## Embedded mode

Pass a `createTheAuth()` instance as `theauth`. For Postgres or MySQL, use this mode.

```typescript
import { createTheAuth } from '@glinr/theauth';
import { createGateway } from '@glinr/theauth-gateway';

const theauth = await createTheAuth({
  database: { provider: 'sqlite', url: 'theauth.db' },
  agents: { enabled: true },
});

const gateway = createGateway({
  upstream: 'http://localhost:8080',
  theauth,
  policies: [
    { path: '/health', public: true },
    { path: '/api/**', requiredPermissions: [{ resource: 'api', actions: ['read'] }] },
  ],
});

await gateway.listen(3000);

// Or mount it in your own server: Web Request in, Response out.
const response = await gateway.handleRequest(request);
```

## Docker and Kubernetes

Run the gateway as a sidecar. Expose only its port.

```dockerfile
CMD ["npx", "@glinr/theauth-gateway", "--config", "/etc/gateway.json", "--database", "/data/theauth.db", "--port", "3000"]
```

## Limits

- **Direct upstream access bypasses it.** Bind the upstream to a private network.
- **No body inspection.** Policies match method and path only.
- **Paths match as the gateway sees them.** Test encoded paths such as `%2F`.
- **HTTP only.** No TLS or WebSocket. Put a TLS proxy in front.
- **Rate limits are in memory, per process.**
- **Audit is not an access log.** It records a permission check, not the decision.
- **Agent revocation is immediate.** MCP OAuth limits: [MCP page](/gateway-mcp#limits).

# MCP server gateway with OAuth 2.1 and RFC 9728

Source: https://docs.theauth.dev/gateway-mcp

```bash
export THEAUTH_MCP_SIGNING_SECRET='the same 32+ character secret as your authorization server'

npx @glinr/theauth-gateway \
  --upstream http://127.0.0.1:3001 \
  --mcp-resource https://mcp.example.com/mcp \
  --mcp-issuer https://auth.example.com \
  --mcp-scope mcp:read \
  --port 3000
```

Needs an [MCP OAuth 2.1](/mcp) authorization server. The upstream never sees a client token.

<Steps>
<Step>

### Set the signing secret

Must match your authorization server's `signingSecret`. Pass it by environment variable, not on the command line.

</Step>
<Step>

### Start the gateway

`--mcp-resource` is the token audience: your authorization server must set it as `aud`. Terminate TLS in front and route the public URL to port 3000.

</Step>
<Step>

### Check the challenge

```bash
curl -i -X POST http://localhost:3000/mcp -d '{}'
# HTTP/1.1 401
# WWW-Authenticate: Bearer resource_metadata="https://mcp.example.com/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/mcp"

curl http://localhost:3000/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/mcp
```

Clients then follow the challenge on their own.

</Step>
</Steps>

## What MCP mode does

| Feature | Behavior |
|---------|----------|
| Protected resource metadata | RFC 9728 at the well-known path and its path suffixed form. `resource` is the public MCP URL, `authorization_servers` your issuer. |
| Token checks | Signature, issuer, expiry, audience (RFC 8707). Tokens for other resources are refused. DPoP-bound tokens work if your auth module has `dpop` enabled. |
| Challenges | `WWW-Authenticate` carries `resource_metadata` and `error`. Scope shortfalls get `403 insufficient_scope`. |
| Scopes | `requiredScopes`, gateway wide or per route. |
| Agent policy | `requiredPermissions` for tokens with an `agent_id` claim. |
| Origin check | Foreign `Origin` rejected (DNS rebinding protection). |
| Streaming | SSE and streamable HTTP both ways, unbuffered. The client token is never forwarded upstream. |

## Per route scopes and agent policy

```json
{
  "upstream": "http://127.0.0.1:3001",
  "mcp": {
    "resource": "https://mcp.example.com/mcp",
    "issuer": "https://auth.example.com",
    "requiredScopes": ["mcp:read"]
  },
  "cors": { "origins": ["https://app.example.com"] },
  "policies": [
    { "path": "/mcp/admin/**", "requiredScopes": ["mcp:write"] },
    {
      "path": "/mcp",
      "method": "POST",
      "requiredPermissions": [{ "resource": "tools", "actions": ["call"] }],
      "rateLimit": { "windowMs": 60000, "max": 120 }
    }
  ]
}
```

```bash
npx @glinr/theauth-gateway --config gateway.json --port 3000
```

`requiredPermissions` checks the agent in the `agent_id` claim, against the gateway's TheAuth database. No `agent_id` means 403. Use `requiredScopes` for tokens not tied to an agent.

## Embedded mode

For a same-process authorization server or a revocation list, pass the real module.

```typescript
import { createTheAuth } from '@glinr/theauth';
import { createMcpModule, createInMemoryJtiDenylist } from '@glinr/theauth/mcp';
import { createGateway } from '@glinr/theauth-gateway';

const mcp = createMcpModule({
  config: {
    enabled: true,
    issuer: 'https://auth.example.com',
    baseUrl: 'https://auth.example.com/api/auth',
    signingSecret: process.env.MCP_SIGNING_SECRET!,
    jtiDenylist: createInMemoryJtiDenylist(),
  },
  // storage callbacks, see the MCP OAuth page
});

const gateway = createGateway({
  upstream: 'http://127.0.0.1:3001',
  theauth,
  mcp: { auth: mcp, resource: 'https://mcp.example.com/mcp', requiredScopes: ['mcp:read'] },
});
await gateway.listen(3000);
```

Only `requireMcpAuth` and `getProtectedResourceMetadata` are used, so a shared-key validation module is enough. The CLI does this.

## Limits

- **Path level only.** Tool names sit in the unparsed JSON-RPC body. Enforce per tool rules upstream or split routes.
- **The CLI cannot see revocations.** Tokens stay valid until `exp`. Use short lifetimes, or embedded mode with a shared `jtiDenylist`.
- **HS256 shared secret.** Anyone holding it can mint tokens. The CLI does not fetch JWKS.
- **Not an authorization server.** Registration, login, consent and issuing stay upstream.
- **Well-known paths are shadowed.** Upstream `/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource` routes never run.
- **Sessions are not bound to tokens.** `Mcp-Session-Id` passes through, and a second authenticated client that learns an ID could use it. Treat IDs as secrets.
- **Audit only with `agent_id`.** Other OAuth tokens are enforced but not logged.
- **Rate limits are in memory, per process.**
- **HTTP only.** No TLS or WebSocket. The legacy stdio transport is out of scope.
- **Not tested with a real MCP client.** Unit and local socket tests only. Add headers missing from the default list to `cors.headers`.

# Overview

Source: https://docs.theauth.dev/adapters/index

## How adapters work

The `@glinr/theauth` package has zero framework dependencies. It operates entirely on the Web platform `Request`/`Response` API. Adapter packages wrap the core and expose framework-idiomatic handlers for authentication, authorization, and MCP OAuth routes.

Because the core uses only Web platform APIs, theAuth runs on edge runtimes without modification: Next.js Edge Runtime, Cloudflare Workers, Deno Deploy, Vercel Edge Functions, and Bun. The Hono and SvelteKit adapters are fully edge-compatible out of the box. The Next.js adapter works on edge when you use `export const runtime = 'edge'` in your route file.

Each adapter follows the same pattern: accept a `theauth` instance, optionally accept a config object, and return something your framework knows how to mount.

```typescript
import { createTheAuth } from '@glinr/theauth';
import { createMcpModule } from '@glinr/theauth/mcp';
import { mcpStore } from './mcp-store.js'; // storage callbacks, see the MCP page

const theauth = await createTheAuth({
  database: { provider: 'sqlite', url: 'theauth.db' },
  baseUrl: 'https://auth.yourapp.com',
});

// optional, enables MCP OAuth endpoints
const mcp = createMcpModule({
  config: {
    enabled: true,
    issuer: 'https://auth.yourapp.com',
    baseUrl: 'https://auth.yourapp.com/api/theauth', // origin plus the mount path
    signingSecret: process.env.MCP_SIGNING_SECRET!, // at least 32 characters
  },
  ...mcpStore,
});
```

Pass `mcp` to the adapter to enable the MCP OAuth 2.1 endpoints under the same mount path. `createMcpModule` comes from `@glinr/theauth/mcp` and takes a config object plus storage callbacks, see [MCP](/mcp).

## Authenticate the management routes

The agent, delegation, audit and dashboard routes (`/agents`, `/delegations`, `/audit`, `/dashboard`, and `POST /authorize`) manage your whole agent fleet, so every adapter requires an authenticated caller. `/authorize/token` (agent bearer token), the MCP endpoints, password reset, email verification and plugin routes are not affected; they carry their own checks.

Pass an `authenticate` function. It receives the standard `Request` and returns `{ id }` for an allowed caller or `null` to reject with 401:

```ts
const authenticate = async (request: Request) => {
  const user = await theauth.auth.resolveUser(request);
  return user?.id === process.env.ADMIN_USER_ID ? { id: user.id } : null;
};

app.route('/api/theauth', theAuthHono(theauth, { authenticate }));
```

`theauth.auth.resolveUser` only consults the `auth.adapter` you configured. If you rely on `auth.session` alone, skip `authenticate` (see next paragraph) or validate the token yourself with `theauth.auth.session.validate(token)`.

If you leave `authenticate` out and `auth.session` is configured on `createTheAuth`, the adapter accepts any valid session (cookie or `Authorization: Bearer <session token>`). That admits every signed-in user, but each one only sees and acts on their own agents, delegations and audit rows. Write your own resolver when admins or service tokens need to reach everything; whatever a custom resolver accepts is unrestricted. If neither is configured, the adapter throws when you create it:

```
[theauth] theAuthHono: the management routes (/agents, /delegations, /audit, /dashboard, /authorize) require authentication, but none is configured.
```

For a local demo you can opt out with `allowUnauthenticated: true`. A warning is logged on startup. Do not ship it.

### Rate limiting and cross-site writes

Every adapter refuses abusive traffic before authentication runs.

- **Rate limits** are per client, in three tiers: token, registration and authorize routes (30 per minute), other writes (120 per minute) and reads (300 per minute). Exceeding one returns `429` with `Retry-After`.
- **Cookie sessions** cannot be used for cross-site writes. A `POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH` or `DELETE` that carries a cookie and no `Authorization` header must come from the adapter's own origin or one listed in `trustedOrigins`. Bearer callers are not affected.

```typescript
app.use("/api/theauth", theAuthExpress(theauth, {
  trustedProxy: { trustedProxyCount: 1 },
  trustedOrigins: ["https://app.example.com"],
  rateLimit: { read: { max: 600, window: 60 } },
}));
```

Two hooks cover the cases the defaults miss. `skip` leaves a request out of rate limiting (health checks, your own network) and `key` replaces the client key, for example to count per tenant:

```typescript
rateLimit: {
  skip: (request, path) => path === "/health",
  key: (request) => request.headers.get("x-tenant"), // null falls back to the client IP
}
```

Set `trustedProxy` so limits apply per client IP. Without it the IP is unknown and callers are split by their credential instead. Counts are kept in the `rateLimit` [secondary storage](/configuration). With the default in-process store each instance counts alone; configure `secondaryStorage: "database"` or a Redis style store and one limit holds across instances. If the store errors, the request is let through so an outage there does not take sign-in down. Use `rateLimit: false` or `csrf: false` to switch either check off.

### Upgrading

Earlier versions mounted these routes with no authentication. After upgrading, pass `authenticate` (or configure `auth.session`) to each adapter call, or add `allowUnauthenticated: true` while you work on it locally.

## Available adapters

| Package | Framework | Mount pattern |
|---|---|---|
| [`@glinr/theauth-hono`](/adapters/hono) | Hono | `app.route('/api/theauth', theAuthHono(theauth))` |
| [`@glinr/theauth-express`](/adapters/express) | Express | `app.use('/api/theauth', theAuthExpress(theauth))` |
| [`@glinr/theauth-nextjs`](/adapters/nextjs) | Next.js App Router | catch-all route `app/api/theauth/[...theauth]/route.ts` |
| [`@glinr/theauth-fastify`](/adapters/fastify) | Fastify | `app.register(theAuthFastify(theauth), { prefix: '/api/theauth' })` |
| [`@glinr/theauth-nuxt`](/adapters/nuxt) | Nuxt (H3) | catch-all file `server/api/theauth/[...].ts` |
| [`@glinr/theauth-sveltekit`](/adapters/sveltekit) | SvelteKit | catch-all route `src/routes/api/theauth/[...path]/+server.ts` |
| [`@glinr/theauth-astro`](/adapters/astro) | Astro | catch-all page `src/pages/api/theauth/[...path].ts` |
| [`@glinr/theauth-nestjs`](/adapters/nestjs) | NestJS | `AuthModule.forRoot({ theauth, mcp })` |
| [`@glinr/theauth-solidstart`](/adapters/solidstart) | SolidStart | catch-all route `src/routes/api/theauth/[...theauth].ts` |
| [`@glinr/theauth-tanstack`](/adapters/tanstack) | TanStack Start | catch-all route `app/routes/api/theauth.$.ts` |

## Endpoints registered

All adapters register the same set of REST routes under `basePath` (default `/api/theauth`):

| Path | Methods | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `/agents` | `GET`, `POST` | List and create agents |
| `/agents/:id` | `GET`, `PATCH`, `DELETE` | Get, update, revoke an agent |
| `/agents/:id/rotate` | `POST` | Rotate an agent's token |
| `/authorize` | `POST` | Authorize an action by agent ID |
| `/authorize/token` | `POST` | Authorize an action by bearer token |
| `/delegations` | `POST` | Create a delegation chain |
| `/delegations/:id` | `DELETE` | Revoke a delegation |
| `/delegations/:agentId` | `GET` | List delegation chains for an agent |
| `/audit` | `GET` | Query audit logs |
| `/audit/export` | `GET` | Export audit logs as JSON or CSV |

When `mcp` is passed, additional endpoints are registered:

| Path | Methods | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server` | `GET` | OAuth 2.1 server metadata (RFC 8414) |
| `/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource` | `GET` | Protected resource metadata (RFC 9728) |
| `/mcp/register` | `POST` | Dynamic client registration (RFC 7591) |
| `/mcp/authorize` | `GET` | Authorization endpoint (PKCE + S256) |
| `/mcp/token` | `POST` | Token endpoint |

<Warning>
  These paths are relative to the mount point, but MCP clients look for the `/.well-known/*` documents at the root of your origin. When you mount the adapter under a prefix such as `/api/theauth`, also serve `mcp.getMetadata()` and `mcp.getProtectedResourceMetadata()` from root-level `/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server` and `/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource` routes. See [MCP](/mcp).
</Warning>

## Using without an adapter

If your framework is not listed, call the module methods directly from any server that handles standard `Request` objects. The `mcp` module from `createMcpModule` does not route URLs for you: you map paths to its methods yourself.

```typescript
import { mcp } from './lib/theauth.js';

async function handler(request: Request): Promise<Response> {
  const url = new URL(request.url);

  if (url.pathname === '/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server') {
    return Response.json(mcp.getMetadata());
  }
  if (url.pathname === '/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource') {
    return Response.json(mcp.getProtectedResourceMetadata());
  }

  // Protect everything else: 401 or 403 responses are built for you
  const check = await mcp.requireScopes(request, ['mcp:read']);
  if (!check.authorized) return check.response;

  return Response.json({ tools: [] });
}
```

You would also route `/mcp/register`, `/mcp/authorize`, and `/mcp/token` to `mcp.registerClient(body)`, `mcp.authorize(request)`, and `mcp.token(request)`, which return a `Result` you turn into a `Response`. The adapters in this table already do that, and the agent REST routes are only available through an adapter.

# Hono

Source: https://docs.theauth.dev/adapters/hono

`theAuthHono(theauth, options?)` returns a `Hono` app instance with all theAuth routes pre-mounted. Use `app.route` to attach it to your main app.

## Install

```bash
pnpm add @glinr/theauth @glinr/theauth-hono hono @hono/node-server
```

## Setup

<Steps>
<Step title="Create the theauth instance">

Create this once and reuse it across your app (e.g. `lib/theauth.ts`):

```typescript
// lib/theauth.ts
import { createTheAuth } from '@glinr/theauth';
import { createMcpModule } from '@glinr/theauth/mcp';
import { mcpStore } from './mcp-store.js'; // storage callbacks, see the MCP page

export const theauth = await createTheAuth({
  database: { provider: 'sqlite', url: 'theauth.db' },
  baseUrl: process.env.AUTH_BASE_URL!,
  mcp: { enabled: true }, // creates the MCP tables
});

// baseUrl is the public origin plus the adapter mount path (default /api/theauth)
export const mcp = createMcpModule({
  config: {
    enabled: true,
    issuer: process.env.AUTH_BASE_URL!,
    baseUrl: `${process.env.AUTH_BASE_URL!}/api/theauth`,
    signingSecret: process.env.MCP_SIGNING_SECRET!, // at least 32 characters
  },
  ...mcpStore,
});
```

</Step>
<Step title="Mount the adapter">

```typescript
// src/index.ts
import { serve } from '@hono/node-server';
import { Hono } from 'hono';
import { theAuthHono } from '@glinr/theauth-hono';
import { theauth, mcp } from './lib/theauth.js';

const app = new Hono();

// Who may call the management routes. Return { id } to allow, null to reject (401).
// resolveUser needs an auth.adapter; with only auth.session, omit authenticate
// and any valid session is accepted.
const authenticate = async (request: Request) => {
  const user = await theauth.auth.resolveUser(request);
  return user ? { id: user.id } : null;
};

// Mount all TheAuth routes (agents, permissions, audit, MCP OAuth)
app.route('/api/theauth', theAuthHono(theauth, { mcp, authenticate }));

serve({ fetch: app.fetch, port: 3000 });
```

</Step>
</Steps>

## Authentication and mount prefixes

`theAuthHono` refuses to start without a way to authenticate callers on `/agents`, `/delegations`, `/audit`, `/dashboard` and `POST /authorize`. Pass `authenticate`, configure `auth.session`, or set `allowUnauthenticated: true` for local development. The full rules and the upgrade note are on the [adapters overview](/adapters#authenticate-the-management-routes).

```typescript
const authenticate = async (request: Request) => {
  const user = await theauth.auth.resolveUser(request);
  return user ? { id: user.id } : null;
};

app.route('/api/theauth', theAuthHono(theauth, { authenticate }));
```

Plugin routes (magic link, email OTP and so on) work under any prefix. The adapter works out the prefix from the request path, so `app.route('/x', theAuthHono(...))` and `app.route('/api/v1/theauth', ...)` both reach `/auth/magic-link/send` at the right place.

## MCP endpoints

Pass `mcp` to enable the full MCP OAuth 2.1 authorization server. All MCP endpoints are mounted under the same `/api/theauth` prefix alongside the REST API:

```typescript
app.route('/api/theauth', theAuthHono(theauth, { mcp, authenticate }));
// registers:
// GET  /api/theauth/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server
// GET  /api/theauth/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource
// POST /api/theauth/mcp/register
// GET  /api/theauth/mcp/authorize
// POST /api/theauth/mcp/token
```

<Info>
  MCP routes include CORS headers (`Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`) and respond to OPTIONS preflight requests automatically.
</Info>

## Management routes and client IP

With the default session guard, a signed-in user only acts on their own agents, delegations and audit rows. A custom `authenticate` resolver is a trust decision and sees everything.

The adapter does not read forwarded headers for the client IP. Behind a proxy, set `trustedProxy` with `trustedProxyCount` or `trustedHeader`, or `ipAllowlist` constraints cannot match.

```ts
app.route('/api/theauth', theAuthHono(theauth, { authenticate, trustedProxy: { trustedProxyCount: 1 } }));
```

On Cloudflare use `trustedHeader: 'cf-connecting-ip'`. Only trust a header your edge overwrites.

## Endpoint reference

| Method | Path | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `POST` | `/agents` | Create an agent |
| `GET` | `/agents` | List agents |
| `GET` | `/agents/:id` | Get an agent |
| `PATCH` | `/agents/:id` | Update an agent |
| `DELETE` | `/agents/:id` | Revoke an agent |
| `POST` | `/agents/:id/rotate` | Rotate token |
| `POST` | `/authorize` | Authorize by agent ID |
| `POST` | `/authorize/token` | Authorize by bearer token |
| `POST` | `/delegations` | Create delegation |
| `GET` | `/delegations/:agentId` | List delegation chains |
| `DELETE` | `/delegations/:id` | Revoke delegation |
| `GET` | `/audit` | Query audit logs |
| `GET` | `/audit/export` | Export audit logs |

## Full example

```typescript
import { serve } from '@hono/node-server';
import { Hono } from 'hono';
import { createTheAuth } from '@glinr/theauth';
import { createMcpModule } from '@glinr/theauth/mcp';
import { mcpStore } from './mcp-store.js'; // storage callbacks, see the MCP page
import { theAuthHono } from '@glinr/theauth-hono';

const theauth = await createTheAuth({
  database: { provider: 'sqlite', url: 'theauth.db' },
  baseUrl: 'https://auth.yourapp.com',
  mcp: { enabled: true }, // creates the MCP tables
});

// baseUrl is the public origin plus the adapter mount path (default /api/theauth)
const mcp = createMcpModule({
  config: {
    enabled: true,
    issuer: 'https://auth.yourapp.com',
    baseUrl: 'https://auth.yourapp.com/api/theauth',
    signingSecret: process.env.MCP_SIGNING_SECRET!, // at least 32 characters
  },
  ...mcpStore,
});

const app = new Hono();

// Who may call the management routes. Return { id } to allow, null to reject (401).
// resolveUser needs an auth.adapter; with only auth.session, omit authenticate
// and any valid session is accepted.
const authenticate = async (request: Request) => {
  const user = await theauth.auth.resolveUser(request);
  return user ? { id: user.id } : null;
};

app.route('/api/theauth', theAuthHono(theauth, { mcp, authenticate }));

app.get('/health', (c) => c.json({ ok: true }));

serve({ fetch: app.fetch, port: 3000 });
```

# Express

Source: https://docs.theauth.dev/adapters/express

`theAuthExpress(theauth, options?)` returns an Express `Router` with all theAuth routes pre-mounted. Use `app.use` to attach it at your chosen path.

## Install

```bash
pnpm add @glinr/theauth @glinr/theauth-express express
pnpm add -D @types/express
```

## Setup

<Steps>
<Step title="Create the theauth instance">

```typescript
// lib/theauth.ts
import { createTheAuth } from '@glinr/theauth';
import { createMcpModule } from '@glinr/theauth/mcp';
import { mcpStore } from './mcp-store.js'; // storage callbacks, see the MCP page

export const theauth = await createTheAuth({
  database: { provider: 'postgres', url: process.env.DATABASE_URL! },
  baseUrl: process.env.AUTH_BASE_URL!,
  mcp: { enabled: true }, // creates the MCP tables
});

// baseUrl is the public origin plus the adapter mount path (default /api/theauth)
export const mcp = createMcpModule({
  config: {
    enabled: true,
    issuer: process.env.AUTH_BASE_URL!,
    baseUrl: `${process.env.AUTH_BASE_URL!}/api/theauth`,
    signingSecret: process.env.MCP_SIGNING_SECRET!, // at least 32 characters
  },
  ...mcpStore,
});
```

</Step>
<Step title="Mount the adapter">

```typescript
// src/index.ts
import express from 'express';
import { theAuthExpress } from '@glinr/theauth-express';
import { theauth, mcp } from './lib/theauth.js';

const app = express();

// Required: parse JSON and URL-encoded bodies before the adapter
app.use(express.json());
app.use(express.urlencoded({ extended: true }));

// Who may call the management routes. Return { id } to allow, null to reject (401).
// resolveUser needs an auth.adapter; with only auth.session, omit authenticate
// and any valid session is accepted.
const authenticate = async (request: Request) => {
  const user = await theauth.auth.resolveUser(request);
  return user ? { id: user.id } : null;
};

// Mount all TheAuth routes
app.use('/api/theauth', theAuthExpress(theauth, { mcp, authenticate }));

app.listen(3000);
```

</Step>
</Steps>

<Warning>
  Call `express.json()` and `express.urlencoded()` before mounting the adapter. The adapter reads `req.body` which requires those parsers to be in place.
</Warning>

## MCP endpoints

Pass `mcp` to enable the MCP OAuth 2.1 authorization server. All MCP endpoints are registered on the same router alongside the REST API:

```typescript
app.use('/api/theauth', theAuthExpress(theauth, { mcp, authenticate }));
// registers:
// GET  /api/theauth/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server
// GET  /api/theauth/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource
// POST /api/theauth/mcp/register
// GET  /api/theauth/mcp/authorize
// POST /api/theauth/mcp/token
```

## Management routes and client IP

With the default session guard, a signed-in user only acts on their own agents, delegations and audit rows. A custom `authenticate` resolver is a trust decision and sees everything.

The adapter does not read forwarded headers for the client IP. Behind a proxy, set `trustedProxy` with `trustedProxyCount` or `trustedHeader`, or `ipAllowlist` constraints cannot match.

```ts
app.use('/api/theauth', theAuthExpress(theauth, { authenticate, trustedProxy: { trustedProxyCount: 1 } }));
```

On Cloudflare use `trustedHeader: 'cf-connecting-ip'`. Only trust a header your edge overwrites. Without `trustedProxy` the adapter uses `req.ip`, which is the socket peer unless your server framework is configured to trust the proxy.

## Endpoint reference

| Method | Path | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `POST` | `/agents` | Create an agent |
| `GET` | `/agents` | List agents |
| `GET` | `/agents/:id` | Get an agent |
| `PATCH` | `/agents/:id` | Update an agent |
| `DELETE` | `/agents/:id` | Revoke an agent |
| `POST` | `/agents/:id/rotate` | Rotate token |
| `POST` | `/authorize` | Authorize by agent ID |
| `POST` | `/authorize/token` | Authorize by bearer token |
| `POST` | `/delegations` | Create delegation |
| `GET` | `/delegations/:agentId` | List delegation chains |
| `DELETE` | `/delegations/:id` | Revoke delegation |
| `GET` | `/audit` | Query audit logs |
| `GET` | `/audit/export` | Export audit logs |

## Full example

```typescript
import express from 'express';
import { createTheAuth } from '@glinr/theauth';
import { createMcpModule } from '@glinr/theauth/mcp';
import { mcpStore } from './mcp-store.js'; // storage callbacks, see the MCP page
import { theAuthExpress } from '@glinr/theauth-express';

const theauth = await createTheAuth({
  database: { provider: 'postgres', url: process.env.DATABASE_URL! },
  baseUrl: process.env.AUTH_BASE_URL!,
  mcp: { enabled: true }, // creates the MCP tables
});

// baseUrl is the public origin plus the adapter mount path (default /api/theauth)
const mcp = createMcpModule({
  config: {
    enabled: true,
    issuer: process.env.AUTH_BASE_URL!,
    baseUrl: `${process.env.AUTH_BASE_URL!}/api/theauth`,
    signingSecret: process.env.MCP_SIGNING_SECRET!, // at least 32 characters
  },
  ...mcpStore,
});

const app = express();
app.use(express.json());
app.use(express.urlencoded({ extended: true }));

// Who may call the management routes. Return { id } to allow, null to reject (401).
// resolveUser needs an auth.adapter; with only auth.session, omit authenticate
// and any valid session is accepted.
const authenticate = async (request: Request) => {
  const user = await theauth.auth.resolveUser(request);
  return user ? { id: user.id } : null;
};

app.use('/api/theauth', theAuthExpress(theauth, { mcp, authenticate }));

app.get('/health', (_req, res) => res.json({ ok: true }));

app.listen(3000, () => {
  console.log('Server running on port 3000');
});
```

# Fastify

Source: https://docs.theauth.dev/adapters/fastify

`theAuthFastify(theauth, options?)` returns an async Fastify plugin. Register it with `fastify.register` and use Fastify's built-in `prefix` option to control the mount path.

## Install

```bash
pnpm add @glinr/theauth @glinr/theauth-fastify fastify
```

## Setup

<Steps>
<Step title="Create the theauth instance">

```typescript
// lib/theauth.ts
import { createTheAuth } from '@glinr/theauth';
import { createMcpModule } from '@glinr/theauth/mcp';
import { mcpStore } from './mcp-store.js'; // storage callbacks, see the MCP page

export const theauth = await createTheAuth({
  database: { provider: 'postgres', url: process.env.DATABASE_URL! },
  baseUrl: process.env.AUTH_BASE_URL!,
  mcp: { enabled: true }, // creates the MCP tables
});

// baseUrl is the public origin plus the adapter mount path (default /api/theauth)
export const mcp = createMcpModule({
  config: {
    enabled: true,
    issuer: process.env.AUTH_BASE_URL!,
    baseUrl: `${process.env.AUTH_BASE_URL!}/api/theauth`,
    signingSecret: process.env.MCP_SIGNING_SECRET!, // at least 32 characters
  },
  ...mcpStore,
});
```

</Step>
<Step title="Register the plugin">

```typescript
// src/index.ts
import Fastify from 'fastify';
import { theAuthFastify } from '@glinr/theauth-fastify';
import { theauth, mcp } from './lib/theauth.js';

const app = Fastify();

// Who may call the management routes. Return { id } to allow, null to reject (401).
// resolveUser needs an auth.adapter; with only auth.session, omit authenticate
// and any valid session is accepted.
const authenticate = async (request: Request) => {
  const user = await theauth.auth.resolveUser(request);
  return user ? { id: user.id } : null;
};

// Use Fastify's prefix option to set the mount path
await app.register(theAuthFastify(theauth, { mcp, authenticate }), {
  prefix: '/api/theauth',
});

await app.listen({ port: 3000 });
```

</Step>
</Steps>

<Info>
  The prefix is controlled by Fastify's `register` options, not by a `basePath` option on the adapter. This is consistent with how Fastify plugins work.
</Info>

## MCP endpoints

When `mcp` is passed, the MCP OAuth 2.1 endpoints are registered on the same plugin. Because Fastify's prefix scopes routes, the well-known paths are served relative to the plugin root:

```
GET  /api/theauth/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server
GET  /api/theauth/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource
POST /api/theauth/mcp/register
GET  /api/theauth/mcp/authorize
POST /api/theauth/mcp/token
```

All MCP routes include CORS headers and respond to OPTIONS preflight requests.

## Management routes and client IP

With the default session guard, a signed-in user only acts on their own agents, delegations and audit rows. A custom `authenticate` resolver is a trust decision and sees everything.

The adapter does not read forwarded headers for the client IP. Behind a proxy, set `trustedProxy` with `trustedProxyCount` or `trustedHeader`, or `ipAllowlist` constraints cannot match.

```ts
await app.register(theAuthFastify(theauth, { authenticate, trustedProxy: { trustedProxyCount: 1 } }), { prefix: '/api/theauth' });
```

On Cloudflare use `trustedHeader: 'cf-connecting-ip'`. Only trust a header your edge overwrites. Without `trustedProxy` the adapter uses `request.ip`, which is the socket peer unless your server framework is configured to trust the proxy.

## Endpoint reference

| Method | Path | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `POST` | `/agents` | Create an agent |
| `GET` | `/agents` | List agents |
| `GET` | `/agents/:id` | Get an agent |
| `PATCH` | `/agents/:id` | Update an agent |
| `DELETE` | `/agents/:id` | Revoke an agent |
| `POST` | `/agents/:id/rotate` | Rotate token |
| `POST` | `/authorize` | Authorize by agent ID |
| `POST` | `/authorize/token` | Authorize by bearer token |
| `POST` | `/delegations` | Create delegation |
| `GET` | `/delegations/:agentId` | List delegation chains |
| `DELETE` | `/delegations/:id` | Revoke delegation |
| `GET` | `/audit` | Query audit logs |
| `GET` | `/audit/export` | Export audit logs |

## Full example

```typescript
import Fastify from 'fastify';
import { createTheAuth } from '@glinr/theauth';
import { createMcpModule } from '@glinr/theauth/mcp';
import { mcpStore } from './mcp-store.js'; // storage callbacks, see the MCP page
import { theAuthFastify } from '@glinr/theauth-fastify';

const theauth = await createTheAuth({
  database: { provider: 'postgres', url: process.env.DATABASE_URL! },
  baseUrl: process.env.AUTH_BASE_URL!,
  mcp: { enabled: true }, // creates the MCP tables
});

// baseUrl is the public origin plus the adapter mount path (default /api/theauth)
const mcp = createMcpModule({
  config: {
    enabled: true,
    issuer: process.env.AUTH_BASE_URL!,
    baseUrl: `${process.env.AUTH_BASE_URL!}/api/theauth`,
    signingSecret: process.env.MCP_SIGNING_SECRET!, // at least 32 characters
  },
  ...mcpStore,
});

const app = Fastify({ logger: true });

// Who may call the management routes. Return { id } to allow, null to reject (401).
// resolveUser needs an auth.adapter; with only auth.session, omit authenticate
// and any valid session is accepted.
const authenticate = async (request: Request) => {
  const user = await theauth.auth.resolveUser(request);
  return user ? { id: user.id } : null;
};

await app.register(theAuthFastify(theauth, { mcp, authenticate }), {
  prefix: '/api/theauth',
});

app.get('/health', async () => ({ ok: true }));

await app.listen({ port: 3000, host: '0.0.0.0' });
```

# NestJS

Source: https://docs.theauth.dev/adapters/nestjs

`AuthModule.forRoot(options)` is a NestJS dynamic module that mounts all theAuth routes as Express middleware. Import it once in your root `AppModule`.

## Install

```bash
pnpm add @glinr/theauth @glinr/theauth-nestjs
```

## Setup

<Steps>
<Step title="Create the theauth instance">

```typescript
// lib/theauth.ts
import { createTheAuth } from '@glinr/theauth';
import { createMcpModule } from '@glinr/theauth/mcp';
import { mcpStore } from './mcp-store.js'; // storage callbacks, see the MCP page

export const theauth = await createTheAuth({
  database: { provider: 'postgres', url: process.env.DATABASE_URL! },
  baseUrl: process.env.AUTH_BASE_URL!,
  mcp: { enabled: true }, // creates the MCP tables
});

// baseUrl is the public origin plus the adapter mount path (default /api/theauth)
export const mcp = createMcpModule({
  config: {
    enabled: true,
    issuer: process.env.AUTH_BASE_URL!,
    baseUrl: `${process.env.AUTH_BASE_URL!}/api/theauth`,
    signingSecret: process.env.MCP_SIGNING_SECRET!, // at least 32 characters
  },
  ...mcpStore,
});
```

</Step>
<Step title="Import AuthModule">

```typescript
// app.module.ts
import { Module } from '@nestjs/common';
import { AuthModule } from '@glinr/theauth-nestjs';
import { theauth, mcp } from './lib/theauth.js';

@Module({
  imports: [
    AuthModule.forRoot({
      theauth,
      mcp,
      authenticate, // who may call /agents, /delegations, /audit, /dashboard
      basePath: '/api/theauth', // default
    }),
  ],
})
export class AppModule {}
```

</Step>
<Step title="Bootstrap">

```typescript
// main.ts
import { NestFactory } from '@nestjs/core';
import { AppModule } from './app.module.js';

async function bootstrap() {
  const app = await NestFactory.create(AppModule);
  await app.listen(3000);
}

bootstrap();
```

</Step>
</Steps>

<Info>
  NestJS uses Express under the hood by default. The adapter mounts an Express Router directly, so no extra configuration is needed.
</Info>

## Route prefix

The default mount path is `/api/theauth`. Change it with the `basePath` option:

```typescript
AuthModule.forRoot({ theauth, basePath: '/auth' })
```

All theAuth routes will then be available under `/auth/*`.

## Without a module

If you prefer to mount routes imperatively in `main.ts` rather than importing a module, use `theAuthMiddleware` directly:

```typescript
// main.ts
import { NestFactory } from '@nestjs/core';
import { AppModule } from './app.module.js';
import { theAuthMiddleware } from '@glinr/theauth-nestjs';
import { theauth, mcp } from './lib/theauth.js';

async function bootstrap() {
  const app = await NestFactory.create(AppModule);
// Who may call the management routes. Return { id } to allow, null to reject (401).
// resolveUser needs an auth.adapter; with only auth.session, omit authenticate
// and any valid session is accepted.
const authenticate = async (request: Request) => {
  const user = await theauth.auth.resolveUser(request);
  return user ? { id: user.id } : null;
};

  app.use('/api/theauth', theAuthMiddleware({ theauth, mcp, authenticate }));
  await app.listen(3000);
}

bootstrap();
```

## MCP endpoints

Pass `mcp` to enable the MCP OAuth 2.1 authorization server:

```typescript
AuthModule.forRoot({ theauth, mcp, basePath: '/api/theauth' })
// registers:
// GET  /api/theauth/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server
// GET  /api/theauth/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource
// POST /api/theauth/mcp/register
```

| `POST` | `/agents/:id/rotate` | Rotate token |

| `POST` | `/authorize/token` | Authorize by bearer token |
| `POST` | `/delegations` | Create delegation |
| `GET` | `/delegations/:agentId` | List delegation chains |
| `DELETE` | `/delegations/:id` | Revoke delegation |
| `GET` | `/audit` | Query audit logs |
| `GET` | `/audit/export` | Export audit logs |
